chapter: Fletcher, Wooding and the Harlem scene
title: Leaving Fletcher in Chicago and the trip home penniless
summary: Refusing to go south, four musicians used their money on the fine, passed the hat in Pittsburgh and played for meals on the train to New York.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: Let me kind of curve this conversation since we're speaking this way, like you say, you did quite a bit of traveling throughout the country. It was the South as well?

Well, that's how come we left Fletcher. We left Fletcher with Ethel Waters in Chicago. That's because -- we was with Fletcher, you know, and I went to Chicago, we were going to play the Grand Theater with Fletcher and Ethel.
This was the early part of '23 or latter

part of '22. I remember -- I'm a little twisted on this. It was before the fall because I went into New York at the Nest in '23, in the fall of '23.. It must have been the first part of the winter of '23 or the latter part of '22. And we left the band after I got out of trouble and paid the fine and got out of trouble for carrying the gun. They were going south, and three of us would not go south -- four of us wouldn't go south, so they had to hire musicians from Chicago to make that tour. And --
So that's as far south as you would go?

Oh, I wouldn't dare go south in those days. I had been south with the circus and that was enough for me. And, what happened was, we - it took all the money that I had and that the four of us had to get the two of us out of jail because we had to pay the policy - Pete and he had to pay the judge, and all that sort of thing. Get us off to keep from doing six months. So we had enough money to get from Chicago to Pittsburgh, the four of us. We didn't have another penny after that. So we went to the hotel where we had stayed previously doing one-night stands in Pittsburgh, and told the man what had happened. "We don't have any money." So, he says, well, stay here and see what I can do. Maybe I -- you want to get to New York." I said, "We've got to get to New York." We didn't have a penny. "Have you got anything to eat?" "No,"

we didn't have anything to eat, so he fed us. He said, "Look, there's a dance down at Duquesne Garden tonight. Why don't you go down there and play. Maybe you can pass the hat or something." So, the trombone player said, "Let's do that." So that night we went down to Duquesne Garden. We told the leader -- and Old Man Bailey went with us and said what had happened. We got up on the stand and played the Tiger Rag with their rhythm section -- we played the solos and passed the hat. Monk, you're sitting there but you're not going to believe this. We got to the penny, to the penny, our fare back to New York, for the four of us. Not one penny over. We had to borrow money from Old Man Bailey to pay our taxi cab fare to go the railroad station. Not one penny over.

Right to the penny. So we got on the train the next morning to go to New York and so we're practicing -- about noon we got out the horns, one was a violin, trumpet, trombone and clarinet. And we're fooling around and one of the porters came through and heard us. He went back and got the steward. The steward said, "Would you boys like to play on the train for dinner?"
You know, it took about 12 hours to go from New York to Pittsburgh on a train. We said, "Yeah, okay, we got nothing to do." He said, "Well, look, I can't pay you

but anything you want to eat you can have." "Okay," you know, we tried to play it cool, but we were so happy we were going to eat. So we went and played for dinner and we got through and had steaks and chicken a la king and anything we wanted to eat. So, when it came time for supper, he said "Same deal goes, fellows." And we played for supper that night, and we ate again.
They didn't allow you to pass the hat?

On the train, no, just food. Let me tell you, so we got to New York and we didn't have enough money to even telephone to tell my father to come down -- we had an old broken down Cadillac then -- telephone daddy to come down to pick up at the station. I had to borrow a nickle from the porter so I could call my father to come and get me at the Pennsylvania Station.
